I spent three days chasing a single ghost checkout bug on STRAYED.

We were setting up our custom payment flow and the checkout was lagging. Users would hit pay, get their money deducted, but the order confirmation screen would just hang. Tbh, it was incredibly frustrating because on paper, everything looked perfectly clean.

The issue turned out to be how we handled Razorpay webhooks. The webhook was triggering a confirmation email before the local database write fully completed. This caused a weird race condition that kept mobile users staring at a spinning loader.

To fix it, we refactored our state machine to prioritize optimistic UI updates. Now, the client assumes success immediately after the gateway callback, while a silent database query handles any delays in the background. Latency dropped to almost zero.

It made me realize how much of good UX is just hiding backend latency from the user.

How do you handle webhook race conditions without breaking your client-side state?

#webdev #javascript #razerpay

Manual data entry in Odoo is the fastest way to lose your mind.

When we launched Prettiva on December 15, we had thousands of fashion variants to upload. Doing this manually inside Odoo takes days of mind-numbing clicking, especially when you have to map every single image to its specific size and color variant.

I got so tired of it after the first ten products that I shut the dashboard down. Instead, I wrote a quick Python Excel parser script.

The script automatically maps our local image hosting paths to the correct Odoo variant columns. It takes a raw spreadsheet and transforms it into an Odoo-friendly format in seconds.

What used to take our team days now gets done in literally under three minutes. Sometimes, taking twenty hours to write a script to avoid ten hours of manual work is actually the smartest decision you can make.

What is the most boring manual task you have automated with a quick script recently?

#python #automation #ecommerce

Standard e-commerce platforms make custom loyalty programs a subscription nightmare.

Since we built STRAYED on MedusaJS, we decided to program our loyalty system from scratch.

I wrote custom logic in our PostgreSQL database to track customer actions, automatically calculating reward points and triggering mystery gift discounts at checkout based on user history. Everything runs natively within our own backend instead of relying on third-party APIs.

It took a bit of extra development time, but our page load speed is incredibly fast, and we have complete control over how we surprise our users.

If you are building e-commerce, at what point do you decide to build custom features instead of installing pre-made plugins?

Waiting for a backend response to update a cart UI feels incredibly outdated.

When you add an item to your cart on Amazon, the UI updates instantly. There is no spinner, no lag, and no waiting for a server confirmation.

I wanted that exact same zero-latency feel for STRAYED.

To get there, I implemented optimistic client-side updates in our frontend. When a user clicks 'Add to Cart', we immediately update the local React State to reflect the new item, while the actual API request to our MedusaJS backend runs silently in the background.

If the server request fails for some rare reason, we gracefully roll back the UI state and show a quick notification. But 99% of the time, the user experiences an instant, snappy transition.

It is a small detail, but these micro-interactions are what separate clean, premium products from clunky web pages.

How do you approach designing optimistic UI states in your frontend applications?

#javascript #webdev #uxdesign
